subject: orthopaedics
title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

steps.tx: **Carpal tunnel syndrome** is the most frequent compressive neuropathy in the human body, arising from elevated hydrostatic tissue pressure within the fibro-osseous canal of the wrist. The carpal tunnel is bounded deeply by the concave carpal bones and volarly by the unyielding transverse carpal ligament. The tunnel transmits nine flexor tendons alongside the median nerve. Compression produces ischaemia, localized demyelination, and axonal injury, leading to sensory disturbance across the radial three and a half digits.
steps.say: Carpal tunnel syndrome represents median nerve entrapment beneath the rigid transverse carpal ligament. Increased compartment pressure impairs endoneurial blood flow, producing pain and paraesthesias throughout the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger.

steps.tx: **Acroparaesthesia** describes the classic nocturnal awakening with tingling, numbness, and burning pain in the thumb, index, and middle fingers. Patients frequently report relief by shaking, flicking, or massaging their hands, an observation known clinically as the flick sign. Sensory symptoms characteristically spare the central thenar eminence because the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises approximately five centimetres proximal to the wrist and travels superficial to the transverse carpal ligament.
steps.say: Patients wake at night with burning tingling in the median nerve distribution, characteristically relieved by shaking their hands. Crucially, the thenar skin sensation is intact because the palmar cutaneous nerve travels outside and superficial to the carpal tunnel.

steps.tx: **Phalen test** evaluates median nerve irritability by requiring the patient to maintain unforced complete palmar flexion of both wrists at ninety degrees for sixty seconds. This maneuver elevates intracarpal pressure up to three-fold and narrows the canal volume, provoking or exacerbating paresthesias in the median nerve territory in positive tests. Durkan carpal compression test applies direct, continuous thumb pressure over the proximal carpal tunnel for thirty seconds, boasting the highest sensitivity and specificity among provocative physical signs.
steps.say: The Phalen maneuver flexes the wrist fully for sixty seconds to reproduce tingling. The Durkan test directly compresses the volar carpal tunnel with the clinician thumb for thirty seconds and offers the highest diagnostic sensitivity for median nerve compression.

vis.title: Diagnostic Provocative Signs in Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
rows: Complete passive wrist flexion for 60 seconds
Direct thumb pressure over canal for 30 seconds
Light percussion over volar carpal ligament

steps.tx: **Thenar atrophy** indicates advanced, chronic motor axonal loss, involving the abductor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis muscles. Physical examination demonstrates flattening of the normally convex thenar contour. Testing abductor pollicis brevis power involves placing the hand flat with the palm facing upward on a desk and instructing the patient to lift the thumb vertically perpendicular to the palm against resistance. Weakness or failure of perpendicular palmar abduction confirms significant motor fascicle denervation.
steps.say: Thenar wasting signals severe, longstanding median nerve motor damage. Test abductor pollicis brevis specifically by asking the patient to raise the thumb straight up towards the ceiling against resistance with the hand flat on a table.

steps.tx: **Nerve conduction studies** provide objective electrodiagnostic quantification of median nerve focal demyelination across the flexor retinaculum. Pathological thresholds include a distal motor latency exceeding 4.2 milliseconds and an orthodromic sensory conduction velocity dropping below 40 meters per second across the carpal segment. In high-resolution neuromuscular ultrasonography, an enlarged median nerve cross-sectional area surpassing 10 square millimeters measured at the level of the pisiform or carpal inlet serves as an accurate morphological diagnostic criterion.
steps.say: Nerve conduction studies establish the diagnosis by showing prolonged distal motor latency over 4.2 milliseconds and slowed sensory conduction. On ultrasound, a median nerve cross-sectional area greater than ten square millimetres at the carpal tunnel inlet confirms entrapment.

vis.title: Electrodiagnostic and Imaging Criteria
rows: Median distal motor latency to APB

steps.tx: **Wrist splints** immobilized in a neutral position between zero and five degrees of extension maintain minimal hydrostatic intracarpal pressure. Wearing neutral splints during sleep prevents wrist hyperflexion or hyperextension postures that exacerbate nerve ischemia, providing significant symptomatic relief in mild to moderate disease. Local corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel, placing twenty to forty milligrams of methylprednisolone just ulnar to the palmaris longus tendon, offers rapid anti-inflammatory reduction of tenosynovial swelling.
steps.say: Initial non-surgical care employs neutral wrist splints at night to keep canal pressure at its lowest baseline. A local corticosteroid injection placed just medial to the palmaris longus tendon relieves tenosynovial swelling and confirms the diagnosis.

left.title: Conservative Stepped Approach
points: Trial period of four to six weeks

right.title: Operative Indications
points: Constant sensory loss on two-point testing

steps.tx: **Carpal tunnel release** constitutes the definitive surgical treatment, indicated for patients exhibiting thenar motor weakness, persistent sensory deficit, or failure of conservative therapy. The operation accomplishes complete longitudinal division of the transverse carpal ligament, expanding canal volume and eliminating compressive pressures. Surgical release can be executed through a standard mini-open palmar incision aligned with the radial border of the ring finger or via minimally invasive single-portal or two-portal endoscopic approaches.
steps.say: Open or endoscopic surgical release fully divides the transverse carpal ligament, immediately relieving median nerve ischaemia. Surgery is urgently indicated whenever objective muscle wasting or dense permanent sensory loss appears.

steps.tx: **Recurrent motor branch** of the median nerve supplies the thenar muscles and exhibits significant anatomical variability that puts it at high risk of iatrogenic transection during carpal tunnel release. In approximately twenty percent of hands, the motor branch exhibits a transligamentous course, piercing directly through the substance of the transverse carpal ligament rather than branching distal to it. Iatrogenic laceration produces immediate paralysis of thumb opposition and palmar abduction, causing permanent severe disability.
steps.say: Always protect the recurrent motor branch to the thenar muscles during release. In one fifth of patients, it takes a transligamentous route directly through the fibers of the transverse ligament, leaving it exceptionally vulnerable to accidental surgical division.
